abstract: Birth marks a profound shift in sensory experience, posing a question: does postnatal brain function represent simply a protracted continuation of prenatal developmental programmes or reflect system-level reconfiguration in response to the demands of the postnatal environment? To answer this, we first characterised functional hierarchies of the newborn human brain, separating sensorimotor from visual, unimodal from associative, and parietal from auditory systems. We then implemented a geometric framework to map global transformations that shape functional connectome hierarchies. We show that greater postmenstrual age at birth was associated with emergence of the frontoparietal and salience networks at the tip of the unimodal-associative hierarchical axis; in contrast, greater postnatal age was associated with increasing polarisation of primary perceptual and sensorimotor systems across functional hierarchies. Sex differences in the neonatal connectome recapitulated patterns associated with postmenstrual age at birth and postnatal age, suggesting more advanced maturation of functional architecture in females than in males. Together, the contrasting effects of prenatal and postnatal age support a model of postnatal reconfiguration of brain function, thereby indicating that birth could mark a transition between distinct modes of the functional organisation.
